16.8.5.2.6 Fridel-Crafts Acylation

Benzene reacts with acid halides (or anhydrides) in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst to give aromatic ketones. For example, benzene reacts with acetyl chloride in the presence of aluminum chloride catalyst to form acetophenone.

In acylation of toluene, virtually all the substitution occurs at 4-position (p-position). The reason that you get virtually none of the o-isomer in this instance is because of the size of the incoming acyl group is very large. For example, reaction of toluene with acetyl chloride in the presence of ferric chloride yield p-methylacetophenone.

The electrophile in Friedel-Crafts acylation is a carbocation, generally called an acylium ion (RCO⁺). Acetyl cation (an acylium ion) is formed by reaction of acetyl chloride with aluminum chloride catalyst. The electrophile acylium ion attack on benzene ring and form aromatic ketone.

Tidbit

Acylation can only be used to give aromatic ketones, but not aldehydes. This is because the formyl chloride (HCOCl) decomposes to CO and HCl under the reaction conditions.

16.8.5.2.7 Substituent Effects

An electrophilic substitution reaction of benzene results only in the formation of one monosubstituted product because all hydrogen atoms of benzene ring are equivalent. However, second substituent can occupy any of the three remaining position to form three isomeric (ortho, meta and para) disubstituted products. It is expected that ortho, meta and para disubstituted products should be formed with ratio of 2:2:1, as given below.

However, in actual practice the disubstituted products are not formed with the above expected percentages. This is because the first substituent (–E₁) effect the ring making the ortho, meta and para position non-equivalent for electrophilic attack. Similarly the first substituent may also increase or decrease the reactivity of ring for second substitution. These effects are called substitution effects.

Types of effects of Substituents

Effect of a substituent already present on the benzene ring on further substitution can be divided into two categories i.e. Orientation Effect and Reactivity Effect.

(A) Directing or Orientation Effect

The first substitutent may direct the incoming electrophile to ortho, meta or para position, depending on the nature of the first substituent. This is called the directing or orientation effect. It has been experimentally observed that some groups, when attached to the benzene ring, direct the second incoming substituent to either ortho and para positions or to the meta position. Thus, the substituents (groups) can be divided into two classes.

The electrophile in this reaction is a methyl cation (a carbocation) formed by reaction methyl chloride with aluminum chloride. The electrophile carbocation then attacks on benzene ring and forms substitution products.

16.8.5.2.6 Fridel-Crafts Acylation

Benzene reacts with acid halides (or anhydrides) in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst to give aromatic ketones. For example, benzene reacts with acetyl chloride in the presence of aluminum chloride catalyst to form acetophenone.

In acylation of toluene, virtually all the substitution occurs at 4-position (p-position). The reason that you get virtually none of the o-isomer in this instance is because of the size of the incoming acyl group is very large. For example, reaction of toluene with acetyl chloride in the presence of ferric chloride yield p-methylacetophenone.

The electrophile in Friedel-Crafts acylation is a carbocation, generally called an acylium ion (RCO⁺). Acetyl cation (an acylium ion) is formed by reaction of acetyl chloride with aluminum chloride catalyst. The electrophile acylium ion attack on benzene ring and form aromatic ketone.

Tidbit

Acylation can only be used to give aromatic ketones, but not aldehydes. This is because the formyl chloride (HCOCl) decomposes to CO and HCl under the reaction conditions.

16.8.5.2.7 Substituent Effects

An electrophilic substitution reaction of benzene results only in the formation of one monosubstituted product because all hydrogen atoms of benzene ring are equivalent. However, second substituent can occupy any of the three remaining position to form three isomeric (ortho, meta and para) disubstituted products. It is expected that ortho, meta and para disubstituted products should be formed with ratio of 2:2:1, as given below.

However, in actual practice the disubstituted products are not formed with the above expected percentages. This is because the first substituent (–E₁) effect the ring making the ortho, meta and para position non-equivalent for electrophilic attack. Similarly the first substituent may also increase or decrease the reactivity of ring for second substitution. These effects are called substitution effects.

Types of effects of Substituents

Effect of a substituent already present on the benzene ring on further substitution can be divided into two categories i.e. Orientation Effect and Reactivity Effect.

(A) Directing or Orientation Effect

The first substitutent may direct the incoming electrophile to ortho, meta or para position, depending on the nature of the first substituent. This is called the directing or orientation effect. It has been experimentally observed that some groups, when attached to the benzene ring, direct the second incoming substituent to either ortho and para positions or to the meta position. Thus, the substituents (groups) can be divided into two classes.
